Case Information: A 32-year-old female presented with a red, swollen plaque on the inner side of her left forearm, which had been present for 10 days. She experienced general discomfort before the appearance of the lesion, followed by itching and a burning sensation at the site. Initially small, the lesion grew to approximately 5 cm by 4 cm. The plaque started as pink-red and changed to a violet color over 10 days, eventually fading within 3 weeks and leaving slight darkening of the skin. She reported having had 15 similar episodes over the past 18 months, with the lesion recurring at the same location and accompanied by mild general symptoms. The severity of these episodes varied, sometimes necessitating the use of antihistamines and oral steroids for relief. Laboratory tests showed normal hemoglobin and total white blood cell counts. The absolute eosinophil count was 440 cells/mm3 (normal range: 40–440 cells/mm3). Other tests, including random blood sugar, liver and kidney function tests, urinalysis, chest X-ray, and antinuclear antibodies, were all normal.
Diagnostic Tests: Histopathologic examination from a biopsy taken from the plaque showed moderately dense superficial and deep perivascular and periappendageal infiltrate of eosinophils and lymphocytes. Several eosinophils were scattered in the interstitium of reticular dermis and around the deep vascular plexus. The papillary dermis showed moderate edema.

Case Information: A 71-year-old right-handed man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and glaucoma experienced progressive stiffness in his right arm and speech difficulties over one year. He visited the emergency department due to speech issues and high blood pressure, but a brain MRI showed no signs of a stroke. Three months later, he exhibited mild guttural speech difficulties, significantly increased muscle tone in his right arm held in flexion, and difficulty extending and abducting his right-hand fingers, although arm strength remained full. Reflexes were slightly brisk in the right arm, with upgoing plantar reflexes on both sides. His gait was characterized by a slightly stooped posture, reduced right arm swing, and mild postural instability, but stride length and gait speed were normal. Orientation, naming, sensory, and cerebellar functions were intact. Previous brain and spinal MRI showed mild subcortical white matter hyperintensities more pronounced on the left, mild temporal lobe atrophy more on the left, and moderate spinal stenosis with severe bilateral C5-C7 foraminal stenosis, worse on the right. An electromyogram (EMG) of the right upper extremity and cervical paraspinal muscles was normal. He received intensive physical, occupational, and speech therapy, which led to some improvement in daily function. Three months later, his speech difficulties worsened, accompanied by right-sided facial droop and swallowing difficulties. The rigidity in his right upper extremity became more pronounced and extended to his right leg. His Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score was 15, with deficits in executive function, attention, visuospatial ability, and delayed recall that did not improve with cueing. A formal speech evaluation revealed a strained, hypernasal, and breathy vocal quality with slow, effortful, and segmented speech. He had frequent misarticulations, imprecise consonants, and produced only one syllable per breath, showing elements of both spastic and flaccid speech difficulties. He also displayed ideomotor apraxia in his right arm. A follow-up EMG of three limbs, cervical and thoracic paraspinal muscles, and tongue performed a year later showed focal denervation in the right flexor carpi radialis but no tongue denervation. A comprehensive laboratory assessment for metabolic, infectious, or inflammatory conditions was negative. A follow-up brain MRI revealed mild progression of atrophy, mainly in the left motor and pre-motor cortex and left temporal lobe.
Diagnostic Tests: A brain fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan demonstrated left hemisphere hypometabolism primarily within frontal lobe, basal ganglia, and thalamus. Hypometabolism of the left anterior temporal lobe was also noted.

Case Information: A 12-year-old boy was bitten by a southern Pacific rattlesnake (Crotalus oreganus helleri) near the lateral malleolus while walking past a tarp in his uncle's garage in southern California. He described the pain in his foot as intense, comparing it to being 'lit on fire and run over by a truck.' The snake was found and identified by a local herpetologist. Initial treatment in the emergency department included intravenous opioids for pain management, CroFab® antivenom [Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (ovine)], and fluid hydration. Vital signs were stable, and coagulation studies showed mildly elevated D-dimer and fibrinogen levels and mild thrombocytopenia, which resolved the next day. Progressive envenoming signs were controlled with two additional doses of antivenom, totaling 14 vials. Two months later, the patient visited a chronic pain specialist with symptoms progressing up the ipsilateral leg to just below the patella, in the distribution of the sural nerve. Physical examination revealed lower extremity edema up to the knee, erythema, hyperalgesia, hot and cold dysesthesia, and motor and sudomotor changes in the area around the original bite site. These symptoms extended up his leg to the subpatellar region.
Diagnostic Tests: Budapest Criteria were met for the presence of edema up to the knee, erythema, hyperalgesia, hot and cold dysesthesia, and sudomotor changes.

Case Information: A 2.5-year-old boy was seen at the Dentistry Department of Pediatric Dentistry Faculty, Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, in June 2011. He exhibited early loss of the mandibular primary canines and the maxillary right primary canine. Clinical examination showed absence of all maxillary and mandibular primary incisors. According to his parents, the primary incisors had not yet emerged. Extraoral examination noted lip eversion and fine hair, with normal eyebrows and eyelashes. There were no issues with heat intolerance or sweating. The toenails were observed to be spoon-shaped and underdeveloped. A panoramic view was not obtained due to the child's lack of cooperation. Examination of the parents' oral health showed normal dentition and no abnormalities in nails, scalp, hair, or eyebrows. There was no family history of similar conditions, except for a cleft palate in one of the maternal cousins.
Diagnostic Tests: Periapical radiography showed primary anterior germs. DNA was isolated from peripheral blood leukocyte collected in EDTA via the standard salting out method. Two coding exons, exon-intron boundaries, and part of 3’-UTR of MSX1 were polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplified, and the amplicons were subjected to mutation analysis by bidirectional direct sequencing (Bioneer, Korea). Regarding the GenBank entry AF426432, one homozygous C>T variant, 6 nucleotides 3’ of the stop codon (3’-UTR) of MSX1, was identified. While control DNA with C/T genotype was semi-digested into three fragments, the patient’s sample (T/T genotype) was not digested by the Avall enzyme.

Case Information: A 24-year-old male Caucasian presented with secondary hypertension that began at age eleven. Despite treatment with four antihypertensive medications (AT1-receptor antagonist, β-blocker, calcium channel antagonist, and doxazosin mesylate), his blood pressure remained high. Initial examination showed a blood pressure of 180/95 mmHg and a heart rate of 82 beats per minute. A 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measurement while on treatment indicated an average blood pressure of 183/98 mmHg with a heart rate of 71 bpm, with no nocturnal dip. Other physical findings were normal. Serum electrolytes were: sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, calcium 2.7 mmol/L, inorganic phosphorus 4.1 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.97 mg/dL. Renal, liver, and thyroid tests were normal. A 24-hour urine analysis showed normal catecholamines and catecholamine metabolites. Plasma renin activity under medication was undetectable (<1 ng/L), and plasma aldosterone concentration was moderately elevated (237 ng/L), while aldosterone urine excretion was within normal limits (0.44 μg/day). MRI showed no adrenal tumor or other abnormalities. Dexamethasone suppression testing (1.5 mg/day for 5 days) normalized plasma aldosterone concentration (132 ng/L) and reduced urine excretion of 18-hydroxycorticosterone (31–4.2 μg/24 h) and 18-hydroxycortisol (1760–110 μg/24 h). Posture testing resulted in an increase in plasma aldosterone concentration to 304 ng/L, a 28% rise.
Diagnostic Tests: The patient's deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) produced the characteristic 3.9-kb product when the 5′ primer for 11β -hydroxlase and the 3′-primer for aldosterone synthase were used for amplification.

Case Information: A 24-year-old male presented with a 15-day history of persistent swelling of the upper lip that ulcerated 2 days prior. He reported no history of trauma, fever, cough, weight loss, or drug or tobacco usage, and his past medical and dental history was non-contributory. The patient was thin built with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Examination revealed a diffuse, non-tender swelling of the lower lip with mild eversion. A reddish-pink granular lesion was observed involving the vermillion border, labial mucosa, floor of the mouth, and mandibular anterior gingiva. The lesion exhibited patchy areas of brown crustation, bleeding, and purulent discharge. A plain chest radiograph and complete hemogram were within normal range. Serologies for syphilis and Leishmania, Mantoux test, and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV were negative.
Diagnostic Tests: An incisional biopsy from the lesion revealed numerous necrotizing epitheloid granulomas with Langhans type giant cells. Ziehl-Neelsen staining showed multiple rods like acid fast bacilli.

Case Information: A 57-year-old male from Monte Dourado, PA, Brazil, was referred for neurological evaluation in Belém, PA, Brazil, due to brachiocrural paresis that had been progressing over three years. Initially, symptoms were noted in the lower limbs, and after one year, the upper limbs also exhibited paresis, along with fasciculations and tremors in the extremities. Subsequently, the patient experienced dysarthria, dysphagia, and sexual dysfunction. Thirty years prior, he had undergone surgery for gynecomastia. Neurological examination revealed impaired gait, inability to walk on tiptoes, proximal muscle atrophy in the upper limbs, and fasciculations in both upper and lower limbs. Reflex testing showed bilateral hyporeflexia in the triceps, biceps, brachioradialis, pronator, and patellar reflexes (grade 1 on the deep tendon reflexes grading scale), with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally (grade 0). Muscle strength was graded as 4 in the bilateral lower limbs and proximal upper limbs according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale. Bulbar involvement was noted with uvula deviation to the right during phonation and tongue atrophy with fasciculations. Surgical scars from the gynecomastia correction were present. In January 2015, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) imaging indicated thinning of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord with slight signal changes in C4, C5, and C6, without contrast enhancement and of nonspecific nature. Electromyography showed diffuse fasciculations in the upper limbs at rest, particularly in the triceps, extensor digitorum, and first dorsal interosseous muscles of the hand, as well as in the tibialis anterior of the lower limbs. Muscle activity was generally reduced, with few motor units displaying increased duration and amplitude. A neuroconduction study of the upper limbs revealed non-excitable sensory conduction and motor conduction with increased latencies of the median nerve bilaterally. Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels were elevated on two occasions: 1757 U/L in June 2015 and 1638 U/L in December 2015.
Diagnostic Tests: Forty-six CAG repetitions were identified.

Case Information: A 75-year-old Japanese man presented with sudden, asymptomatic gross hematuria. Imaging studies, including ultrasonography and abdominal X-ray, indicated the presence of a bladder calculus. Further evaluation with computed tomography (CT) revealed a 1.8 cm intramural calculus in the right ureter and a well-defined, hypervascular mass approximately 2.1 cm in size at the right trigone of the urinary bladder. Both kidneys showed no signs of hydronephrosis. Cystoscopy was performed, revealing a non-papillary nodular mass at the right trigone, covered by normal urothelium and suggesting a submucosal location. The mucosa was elevated behind the mass, but the right ureteral orifice and calculus were not visible preoperatively. CT indicated that the mass was adjacent to the calculus, potentially obstructing its passage. Magnetic resonance imaging showed no invasive growth. Urine cytology results were negative for malignant cells. The patient underwent transurethral resection (TUR) of the mass, which allowed visualization of the right ureteral orifice and the intra-ureteral calculus. Subsequently, transurethral lithotripsy was performed. The patient recovered without perioperative complications and has remained free of recurrence for 5 months.
Diagnostic Tests: On histologic examination, the urothelium was largely denuded; however, residual urothelium showed no atypia. In the submucosal lesion, we observed spindle-shaped to oval-shaped cells that had mildly hyperchromatic nuclei and eosinophilic elongated or tapering cytoplasm arranged in loose fascicles or perivascular whorls around often-hyalinized blood vessels or in a vague storiform-growth fashion, embedded in variably fibromyxoid or edematous stroma associated with dilated thin-walled blood vessels. Mitotic figures are rare. On immunohistochemical examination, the tumor cells were positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin (SMA), desmin, CD34, and h-caldesmon, and CD99 was weakly and focally expressed. The cells were negative for S-100, CAM5.2, AE1/AE3, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), STAT6, MUC4, and claudin-1.

Case Information: The patient is a 13-month-old male of Chinese descent who was referred for genetic evaluation due to recurrent fever. He is the only child of healthy, non-consanguineous parents with no family history of genetic diseases. Pregnancy was uncomplicated, and no abnormalities were noted at birth. At 7 months old, the patient experienced recurrent fever (8 episodes within two months) with a maximum temperature of 39.2°C and a persistent upper respiratory tract infection. A small facial rash appeared following the fever. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable, with no palpable lymph nodes. Laboratory tests revealed a significant increase in lymphocyte proportion (84.8%, normal range 40-70%) with normal morphology and total white blood cell count (9.67*10^9/L). The CD19+ B cell population was elevated (3,432 cells/μL, normal range 240-1,317 cells/μL), and NK cell proportion was decreased (3.03%). The patient received immunizations and symptomatic treatments but no special treatment. Over the next six months, periodic fever episodes continued every 8 days, lasting 2-3 days each. At 13 months old, the patient was admitted again for recurrent fever. Routine blood tests and immunological investigations showed increased lymphocyte proportion and CD19+ B-cells, with decreased hemoglobin level (90g/L, normal range 110-149g/L).
Diagnostic Tests: A bone marrow biopsy showed hyperplastic anemia. An IgH rearrangement experiment indicated that the patient’s B cells were polyclonal. An abdominal CT scan showed multiple mesenteric lymphadenopathies. An ultrasound examination revealed a normal spleen size and an accessory spleen at the hilum.

Case Information: A 44-year-old woman experienced recurring pain in the right side of her lower jaw for six years. Throughout this period, she underwent various evaluations, including a biopsy of the jaw that did not reveal any abnormalities. Due to increasing pain, she received biphosphonate treatment for one year and had two local excisions of the lesion in her right jaw. After the second excision, she was free of pain for 10 days, but the pain subsequently returned. Eighteen months following her second jaw surgery, she was referred to our orthopedic outpatient clinic for assessment of pain in her left thigh bone. Laboratory tests, including ESR, CRP, and CBC, were within normal limits. X-rays of the femur revealed a single area of increased bone density with thickening of the cortex and new bone formation on the outer layer of the bone.
Diagnostic Tests: Technetium99 scan showed multiple locations of active uptake, including the right mandible, anterior chest wall, left pubic bone and left femur. Biopsy and cultures were negative for malignancy or infection.

Case Information: A 48-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 2-month history of recurrent abdominal pain, which had worsened over the past 2 weeks. He had previously undergone an exploratory laparotomy for acute diffuse peritonitis 50 days prior at a local hospital. During the surgery, numerous 0.2–0.4 cm yellow-white tubercles were observed on the surface of the congestive small intestine, colon, appendix, greater omentum, and mesenterium, particularly in the distal ileum, without any apparent perforation. Rapid pathology of the appendix and omentum indicated acute nonspecific inflammation, and intestinal tuberculosis was initially suspected. Saline and metronidazole were used for irrigation, and abdominal drainage was placed. The patient was discharged with intermittent slight abdominal pain on the 15th day post-operation. Twenty days later, he experienced sudden severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever (39°C). He was readmitted to the local hospital and subsequently transferred to our ICU due to worsening condition. Physical examination revealed significant abdominal tenderness, rebound tenderness, and weakened bowel sounds. Additionally, generalized skin eruptions with an atrophic porcelain-white center surrounded by an erythematous rim were noted on the trunk and extremities, measuring 0.2–1.2 cm. The patient had no history of chronic diseases, alcohol use, family history, herbal agents, or suspected drug use. Laboratory tests and radiographic results were as follows: WBC 8.65*10^9/L (3.5–9.5*10^9/L), NEUT% 0.938 (0.40–0.75), procalcitonin 171.45 ng/ml (0–0.05 ng/ml), HBV-DNA 9.15E+08 IU/ml (<5.0E+02 IU/ml). Tuberculin test, Widder test, anti SS-A, and SS-B antibodies were negative. ANA was 1:100 weakly positive, and Anti Ro-52 antibodies were positive. Computed tomography revealed a small amount of free air bubble, edema, thickening of the small bowel wall, and massive seroperitoneum. An exploratory laparotomy was performed due to the primary diagnosis of Crohn's disease with intestinal perforations. During the operation, more than 100 whitish-yellow plaques, dozens of intestinal perforations, and purulent materials were found. Two meters of the perforated small bowel were resected, and the seromuscular layer was sutured in the wafery areas, followed by enterostomy and abdominal drainage tube placement. On the 5th day post-operation, intestinal contents drained again, indicating recurrence of perforation. Attention was then directed towards the correlation between the perforation and skin lesions.
Diagnostic Tests: Biopsy of skin eruption showed atrophy of epidermis, hyperplasia and collagen of dermal fibrous tissue, degeneration of elastic fibers, significantly reduction and partial necrosis of skin appendages, fibrinoid necrosis in small vessels of the deep dermis and thrombosis in local lumen. Histopathology of the resected intestine showed edema and hyperaemia, thrombus organization of both tiny artery and veins lumen with acute and chronic inflammatory cell infiltration.

Case Information: A 19-year-old female presented with pain in the mandibular anterior region for the past 2 days. She is one of two siblings from non-consanguineous parents, with no family history of orofacial or acral malformations. Her antenatal, neonatal, and infancy periods were uneventful. At the age of 7, she underwent surgical management for an atrial septal defect. She reported menstrual irregularities, with menarche occurring at age 16. She is moderately built, well-nourished, and appears to have normal intelligence. Her height is 167 cm (75th percentile), while her weight (42 kg) and head circumference (20 inches) are both below the 3rd percentile. General physical examination showed broad halluces bilaterally with valgus deformity and dysmorphic nails. There is duplication of the 5th toe on the right foot with syndactyly of the supernumerary digit with the 5th toe. Flexion contraction of the 4th and 5th toes on the left foot and the 4th toe on the right foot was noted. The upper limbs are normal except for a broadened right thumb and nail, and bilateral clinodactyly. No functional deficits in the hands or feet were observed. Extra-oral examination revealed an acrocephalic skull, flattened frontal and occipital regions, and a low hairline. The patient has a leptoprosopic flat face with mild maxillary hypoplasia, relative mandibular prognathism, and a prominent chin. An increased gonial angle was noted on profile view. The nose is long, thin, and pointed with a flattened nasofrontal angle, presenting as a wide root of the nose. Thick eyebrows, prominent eyelashes, mild convergent strabismus, and marginal hypertelorism were observed. Intra-oral examination showed a high arched palate and generalized enamel hypoplasia. The patient is currently undergoing orthodontic treatment for arch crowding and has an anterior deep bite with 100% overlap of mandibular teeth. She has a history of endodontic treatment and apicoectomy of teeth 31 and 41, and currently reports pain in the same region along with vestibular obliteration and tenderness.
Diagnostic Tests: Orthopantomogram confirmed a cystic lesion in mandibular anterior region, increased gonial angles bilaterally and occlusal plane irregularities. Further radiographic examination of craniofacial skeleton (P-A skull and Lateral skull radiographs) revealed evidence of coronal sutural synostosis with prominent copper beaten appearance, flattened occiput and frontal bones, shallow orbits, gross prognathism with obtuse mandibular plane angle, maxillary sinus hyperpneumatization and falx calcification. Hand and wrist radiograph showed short and broad distal phalynx of right thumb, however all bones were otherwise normal. Radiograph of feet revealed duplication of distal phalynx of halluces and valgus deformity at distal interphalyngeal joint bilaterally. There was also evidence of partial duplication of 5th toe; Y-shaped proximal phalynx with one supernumerary phalynx in postaxial position exhibiting soft tissue syndactyly with 5th toe. Fourth and fifth digits of left foot were bent in clinically fixed flexion.

Case Information: A 17-year-old male presented with painful and tender diffuse erythema and swelling, accompanied by a necrotic lesion on the scrotum for three days. One week prior to these symptoms, he had visited the emergency room with fever and sore throat and was prescribed oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid. Physical examination revealed a well-demarcated necrotic lesion approximately 2 cm in size on the anterior scrotum. The lesion was confined to the scrotum, and there was no crepitus in the inflamed tissues. The patient reported no history of local trauma, sexual activity, or other predisposing factors. Laboratory tests showed neutrophilic leukocytosis with a count of 16,430×10^6/L (normal <10,000×10^6/L), elevated C-reactive protein at 70.1 mg/L (normal <5.0 mg/L), and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 32 mm/h (normal <15 mm/h). Scrotal ultrasonography indicated edematous skin thickening and increased vascularity. Blood cultures, urine cultures, and bacterial cultures of the skin were all negative. Serological tests for syphilis and Rickettsia tsutsugamushi antibodies were also negative. Evaluation for sexually transmitted diseases yielded no specific findings.
Diagnostic Tests: The skin biopsy of the scrotal ulcer showed epidermal necrosis and dermal neutrophilic infiltration.

Case Information: A 39-year-old Caucasian male visited our outpatient clinic with seven painless, non-itchy papules that developed within a recent tattoo. These papules emerged approximately three weeks after the patient received a large tattoo on the front side of his right thigh. Initially, the lesions exhibited rapid growth, which later stabilized. Upon physical examination, the papules were found to be unilateral, erythematous, and dome-shaped, with sizes ranging from 4 mm to 1 cm in diameter. Five of the seven lesions were located within the red-inked area of the tattoo, while the remaining two were within the black/gray-inked area. Most of the papules had a thin crust on their surface. The patient reported no previous medical conditions and no additional symptoms. He had received multiple tattoos in the past without any issues and reported no recent sun exposure.
Diagnostic Tests: An excisional biopsy revealed well-circumscribed symmetric tumors with a central keratin-filled crater. The cytologic atypia was mild and the tumors were accompanied by neutrophilic microabscesses and a mixed cell infiltrate.

Case Information: A 23-year-old male army officer visited the clinic with complaints of decreased visual acuity in his left eye over the past 5 months. He had no prior history of eye diseases or surgeries and reported no symptoms such as itching, redness, photophobia, or tearing. Clinical evaluation showed his best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 with −4.50 sph −0.75 cyl 40° in the right eye. The BCVA in the left eye was 20/300 and could not be improved with a refractive correction of −19.00 sph −4.25 cyl 45°. Intraocular pressures measured by a noncontact tonometer were 6 mm Hg in both eyes. Examination of the anterior ocular segment using a slit lamp was unremarkable, with clear cornea and lens, and no signs of inflammation in the anterior chamber. Pupils were equal in diameter and reactive to light, with no relative afferent pupillary defects observed. Dilated fundus examination showed no edema, exudation, or abnormalities in the retina or optic papilla. B-ultrasound scanning revealed no obvious morphological changes in either eye. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) showed no detachment, schisis, or holes in the macular retina, with foveal thickness measured at 259 μm in the right eye and 252 μm in the left eye. The thickness of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer was within normal limits in both eyes. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) showed no leakage of fluorescence in any phase in either eye, and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) revealed no abnormalities. Electroretinography (ERG) performed with a Ganzfeld stimulator showed no significant changes in amplitude and peak time in both dark-adapted and light-adapted responses, with comparable data between both eyes. Pattern visual evoked potentials (PVEP) recorded a slightly reduced amplitude and delayed peak time in the P100-wave of both the 1° and 0.25° PVEP in both eyes, with the delayed peak time more pronounced in the right eye and the reduced amplitude more pronounced in the left eye. Flash visual evoked potentials (FVEP) showed reproducible and reliable waveforms in both eyes, with the amplitude and peak time of the P2-wave within normative ranges and comparable between both eyes.
Diagnostic Tests: An asymmetrical bowtie pattern of the cornea was found in both eyes, which was more obvious in the OS.

Case Information: The patient is a 17-year-old Caucasian female who began experiencing upper extremity symptoms at 10.5 years old. Initially, she had mild difficulty extending the left index finger, which progressed to include the right middle finger after one year. By age 12, she developed more noticeable hand weakness, predominantly on the left side. The weakness worsened in cold weather, and her hands were often cold and sweaty. No sensory deficits were observed. There was no history of cervical trauma, but she experienced a growth spurt in the year before symptom onset, growing approximately 8 cm (between the 75th and 90th percentile for growth velocity). There was no family history of neuromuscular disorders. A neurological examination at age 13 revealed significant weakness (MRC 2 to 3−) in the extension of the index and middle fingers bilaterally and in the abduction of the left thumb. There was also weakness (MRC 3+ to 4) in the extension of the ring and little fingers bilaterally, abduction of the right thumb, and abduction and adduction of the left fingers II-V, as well as flexion of the left fingers II-V. Postural tremor and poly-mini-myoclonus of the fingers on extension were observed. There was marked wasting of the right thenar and mild wasting of other intrinsic hand muscles. Muscle strength in wrist flexion and extension, pronation, and supination of the forearms, flexion and extension of the elbow, and shoulder abduction was normal. Sensory deficits were absent, and deep tendon reflexes were intact. Neurological examination of the lower extremities was normal. Cervical spine motility and forward flexion of the whole spine were normal. A motor deficit affecting roots C7 to T1, more pronounced on the left side, was noted. At age 13, her height was 175 cm (5 cm above the 97th percentile), and her weight was 58 kg (75th–90th percentile). By age 14, the pattern of weakness and wasting remained unchanged, though the severity of weakness had slightly increased, stabilizing over the last six months. Follow-up examinations in subsequent years showed no further changes in the pattern or extent of weakness or wasting.
Diagnostic Tests: Nerve conduction studies of the median and ulnar nerves showed reduced compound motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) and a slightly reduced motor conduction velocity on the left side. No conduction blocks were found and sensory nerve conduction studies of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves were normal. Nerve conduction studies of the right peroneal nerve were normal. Needle electromyography of the first, left interosseus muscle showed high-amplitude, long-duration MUAPs indicating chronic denervation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cervical spine in an orthotopic head position and under head anteflexion showed flattening and a slight intramedullary signal alteration of the myelon between segments C5 and C7.

Case Information: A 10-month-old male presented with skin peeling confined to the hands and feet, first observed at 2 months of age. The condition was noted to worsen with exposure to heat and humidity, but not due to mechanical trauma. The patient was born following a normal pregnancy and delivery, with non-consanguineous parents and no relevant family history. Physical examination revealed erythematous erosions with peripheral desquamation on both palms and soles, along with a flaccid blister on the right-hand finger. Mycological tests on the palms and soles returned negative results. The mother declined a skin biopsy from the edge of a fresh blister for further examination.
Diagnostic Tests: In the index patient, we detected two heterozygous TGM5 mutations: c.2T>C, p.M1T in exon 1 and c.337G>T, p.G113C in exon 3. The father is a heterozygous carrier of the mutation c.2T>C, p.M1T and the mother is a heterozygous carrier of the mutation c.337G>T, p.G113C. No other mutations were disclosed in the analyzed regions.

Case Information: A 5-month-old male, born at full term via cesarean section to nonconsanguineous parents, was admitted due to developmental delays. The mother had taken antiabortion medication early in the pregnancy. There was no family history of developmental delays or seizures. At 5 months, the child was unable to lift his head or roll over. Physical examination revealed wide-set eyes, a high palatal arch, polydactyly of the right little finger, and polydactyly and syndactyly of both little toes. The grandfather had polydactyly of the right hand. Chromosome analysis showed a normal male 46, XY karyotype. Brainstem auditory evoked potential (BAEP) testing indicated moderate hearing loss in the left ear. Visual-evoked potential testing showed abnormalities in the bilateral visual pathways. Brain MRI revealed high signal intensity in the bilateral parietal white matter on T2-weighted images, along with ventricular enlargement and extracerebral space widening.
Diagnostic Tests: Increased pyrimidine and metabolite levels in urine were detected.

Case Information: DF, a 64-year-old right-handed male IT technician, began experiencing progressive changes in behavior and emotional stability at the age of 61. Over the next two years, these issues extended to other cognitive areas such as memory and language, with noticeable difficulties in word finding. Additionally, there was an increase in behavioral issues, including excessive oral tendencies and significantly inappropriate actions.
Diagnostic Tests: MRI indicated clear bilateral frontotemporal involution with left frontal predominance.

Case Information: A 36-year-old female patient reported experiencing right ankle pain for the past four years. She had significant weight loss and began physical activity shortly before the onset of symptoms. There was no history of trauma. Initially, she was treated for synovitis with physical therapy, which did not yield significant improvement. She reported paraesthesia along the posterior and medial aspects of the ankle and foot, with symptoms worsening by the end of the day and episodes of cramping in the foot. Physical examination showed a positive dorsiflexion-eversion test that caused numbness in the foot. Tinel's sign was also positive. The range of motion in the ankle was limited due to pain, which was rated 8 on the Visual Analog Score (VAS). The patient had a preoperative score of 40 points according to the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS). Bilateral electromyography (EMG) revealed abnormal neurophysiologic parameters in the adductor hallucis and adductor digiti quinti muscles compared to the asymptomatic side. Initial plain radiographs identified a significant (1.8 cm) posterior bone fragment associated with the talus.
Diagnostic Tests: CT scan showed the presence of an articulated accessory bone. MRI disclosed the presence of an inflammatory process, bone fragment covered with cartilage, and a degenerative synchondrosis as a consequence of posteromedial impingement.
